conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers adjust emotionally after birth. I’ll be guiding you through the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief set of 10 questions we use to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can be sure you’re getting the support you need.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and the care team, and there are no right or wrong answers. We just want to understand what’s been on your mind and how we can help. If at any point you need a break or want to skip a question, let me know—we’ll go at your pace.  

When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first one.  

**Question 1:** Over the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly... not very much. I can maybe crack a smile if my husband makes a joke, but even then it feels forced. Most of the time I’m just too tired or worried to find anything funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often… maybe once or twice the whole week, and even then it felt kind of fake, like I was just pretending to laugh so nobody would worry.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week nothing sounds appealing. I still do them because I think I “should,” but it feels flat, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. Yesterday the baby was fussy and I kept thinking it must be because I’m not soothing him right, or my milk isn’t good enough. I know it’s probably not true, but the guilt just pops up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke, or I’ll lie down and can’t stop picturing him stopping breathing. Nothing’s actually wrong, but the thoughts just loop and I can’t shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. A couple of nights I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel like the walls are closing in—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m terrified something awful is about to happen even though I know there’s no real danger. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s awful while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. Everything feels like a mountain—folding a load of laundry, answering a text, even just getting a glass of water. I keep thinking, “How am I supposed to do all of this every single day?” Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at the mess because I don’t know where to start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop. I replay every little thing I did with the baby—did I burp him long enough, was the swaddle too tight—and by the time I calm myself it’s been an hour or more. Then I drift off only to jerk awake sure I heard him cry, even when the monitor’s quiet.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, that’s how I spend most of the day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest, and it just stays there. Even when I’m holding the baby and he’s smiling, I feel this ache inside. I keep telling myself I should be happy, but the sadness feels glued to me.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week. It’s usually when the baby won’t settle and I’m running on no sleep—everything just piles up and the tears start coming. I try to hide it so my older kid doesn’t see, but yeah, it’s happened.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Yeah… it’s popped into my head once or twice, like “what if I just weren’t here.” I don’t have a plan or anything, and I’d never leave my kids, but the thought flashes in for a second and scares me.

You've shared how the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy-laughing feels forced, nothing brings pleasure, and guilt or worry hijack even quiet moments. The constant <sym>sadness</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, and exhaustion have made ordinary tasks feel impossible, yet you keep trying for your children.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only once or twice in the week and describes the laughter as forced and insincere, aligning closely with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, doing activities only out of obligation with no pleasure</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame that occurs "a lot" and gives examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries despite no real danger, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with chest tightness and breathlessness occurring 'quite a lot' (multiple nights), matching 'Yes, quite a lot</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive overwhelm ('most of the time') with routine tasks feeling insurmountable, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries preventing sleep onset and repeated awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, persistent sadness that dominates most of the day, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Core symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: depressed mood most of the day (<quote>weight on my chest</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>nothing sounds appealing</quote>), sleep disruption linked to rumination, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and recurrent panic. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental health specialist
2. Complete safety plan and remove potential means of self-harm; involve trusted adult support
3. Consider starting evidence-based therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression)
4. Discuss risks/benefits of compatible antidepressant medication with prescriber
5. Schedule daily check-ins by phone/text with partner, family, or friend until mood stabilises
6. Encourage 15-minute outdoor daylight walks and balanced snacks to support circadian rhythm and energy
7. Provide 24-h crisis lines (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and local emergency numbers
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  

Date: [today]  
Source: self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  
Gestational weeks postpartum: [not specified]  

A. Areas endorsed above threshold  
- Anhedonia (marked loss of interest/pleasure)  
- Persistent low mood, described as “weight on chest” most of the day  
- Daily crying spells  
- Sleep disturbance clearly linked to ruminating worries, not solely infant care demands  
- Excessive inappropriate guilt (“my milk isn’t good enough”) with self-blame for infant fussiness  
- Recurrent intrusive anxiety/panic episodes without external trigger (heart racing, chest tightness, fear of catastrophe)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks “most of the time”  
- Passive suicidal ideation (“what if I just weren’t here”; denies plan/intent)  

B. Pattern summary  
Consistent picture of moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety; functional impairment evident in self-care, household management, and emotional availability to older child.  

C. Safety flag  
Positive for passive self-harm thoughts; no expressed intent, plan, or protective neglect toward infants.  

D. Screening significance / next considerations  
Score profile suggests further evaluation for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset and comorbid Anxiety Disorder. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options (evidence-based therapy ± medication) at earliest opportunity.
